newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Swire perpetual bond cheaper than equity.
newsitem.headline: Swire perpetual bond cheaper than equity.

text.p: Asia's first perpetual bond issue attracted a variety of investors and saved money for its blue chip borrower Swire Pacific Ltd.

"In terms of our calculations, the cost of the perpetual bond is significantly less than equity, particularly after tax," said Martin Cubbon, finance manager at Swire Pacific, which is listed in Hong Kong.
"You don't get a tax deduction for paying dividends and this issue obviously is tax deductible," he said.
But even without the tax benefits, raising money through the bond issue is cheaper than issuing stock, Cubbon said. The bond also helped the company expand its investor base, he said.
The US$300 million bond issue was launched Thursday morning via lead manager Merrill Lynch.
The bonds have a coupon of 9.33 percent and the issuer has the right to call them back from bondholders at par after 10 years and thereafter annually.
If the bonds are not called, they never mature.

Undated or perpetual debt ranks lower than senior debt on a Hong Kong company's balance sheet, but senior to equity. Consequently, the issue has been rated A-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp and Baa1 by Moody's Investors Service Inc. These ratings are one grade below Swire's senior debt ratings
Cubbon said the perpetual bond had some of the attractive features of an equity issue while offering the cost advantages of a bond.
"The issue has qualities of equity that we like, with deferred payments and subordination and perpetuity, but we only pay a fixed coupon," he said.
An equity analyst at a European firm in Hong Kong said the bond clearly will be cheaper for Swire over time.

"I think in the very short term it would be a bit cheaper to use equity, but because of the growth in earnings equity will become more expensive for Swire looking out beyond the end of this year," he said.

Merrill Lynch said that about 50 percent of the bond placed with investors in Asia, 10 percent in Europe and 40 percent in the U.S. The issue size was increased to US$300 million from US$150 million as a result of increased demand.
Most Asian bankers had expected the issue to place well in the U.S., where institutional investors are comfortable with long-term paper in general and are familiar with perpetuals.
The response in Asia, where most debt paper is short-dated and undated debt paper is mostly unknown, was more surprising.

"The issue might have gone into a few of the trading portfolios in some of the banks and to some of the fund managers, which would treat it as quasi equity," said a syndicate manager at a European bank here.
The high coupon and the Swire name would be the main attraction for Asian investors, bankers said.
"Anyone that knows the Swire group in the stock market would be interested," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
"And you are talking about a minimum return of 9.33 percent. I don't think that in the stock market you can actively speculate on that type of return," she said.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6371
